items.title: Stefon Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2020
items.q: I think we were in a space where we needed to be able to stand up, just like James Brown said, “Say it loud/I’m black and I’m proud.”

ctx.x: I’m glad you said that, because it seems there is so much to reflect in the arts now, maybe just so many things that are happening all at the same time, yet over my shoulder are Lester Young and Count Basie, and incredible to think that their music at the time was probably eighty years ago. And do you feel that what they were doing carried as much significance to the community as what you are doing?

Well that’s a tough question because those are my heroes so I’m doing what I can to gain a seat next to them even if it’s like twenty levels down. I just want to be as close to those icons as possible. But what I will say is, as we look at the development of our art form in this country, and we look at the effect of institutionalization on the art form. So when you’re looking at Count Basie or Lester Young, this is before jazz was inside of conservatories and music programs. So the music was really primarily…
Yeah. “Bigger than the notes” I like that.
